<ol>
<li>Inertia: every spinning machine slows together and gives up stored energy (the first seconds).</li>
<li>Primary response: governors on plants holding reserve add power and stop the fall (seconds).</li>
<li>Secondary response: automatic generation control raises reserve plants until 60 Hz returns (minutes).</li>
<li>Last line: if the fall reaches 59.3 Hz, relays disconnect a block of customers automatically.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you trip the plant yourself, set the inertia and the reserve, and step through a real night in Texas.</p>
</div>

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="l3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Frequency</dt><dd>The grid's pulse, 60 Hz in North America; it falls whenever supply is short of demand.</dd>
<dt>Inertia</dt><dd>Energy stored in spinning machines; it slows the fall but cannot stop it.</dd>
<dt>Primary response</dt><dd>Governors add power within seconds and stop the fall at its lowest point, the nadir.</dd>
<dt>Secondary response</dt><dd>Automatic generation control brings frequency back to 60 Hz within minutes.</dd>
<dt>Reserve</dt><dd>Spare capacity held back on running plants; every layer after inertia draws on it.</dd>
<dt>Automatic load shedding</dt><dd>The last line: relays cut a block of customers at 59.3 Hz to save the rest of the grid.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The first second and where the fall stops, in two lines</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Let $f_0 = 60$ Hz, $\Delta P$ the lost power in MW and $E$ the stored rotational energy in MW·s (1 GW·s = 1,000 MW·s). In the first instant only inertia acts, so the [rate of change of frequency]{.lx-term term="rocof"} is

$$\frac{df}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} = -\frac{f_0\,\Delta P}{2E} = -\frac{60 \times 100}{2 \times 16{,}000} \approx -0.19 \text{ Hz/s}.$$

Halve $E$ and the fall is twice as fast. Once governors have caught up, the frequency settles where the governors' extra output, $K$ MW per Hz of drop, and the load's own relief, $D$ MW per Hz, cover the lost power:

$$\Delta f = \frac{\Delta P}{K + D} = \frac{100}{600 + 80} \approx 0.15 \text{ Hz}, \quad f \approx 59.85 \text{ Hz}.$$

$K = 600$ MW/Hz is what a 5% **droop** setting gives on 1,800 MW of plants: a 5% drop in frequency (3 Hz) would call for their full output. All Plains Grid numbers are illustrative.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The swing equation behind the trace</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

With $\Delta f = f - f_0$ and $M = 2E/f_0$ (MW·s per Hz), the page integrates, in 10 ms steps,

$$M\,\frac{d\Delta f}{dt} = \min\big(R,\; p_g + p_a\big) + p_b - D\,\Delta f - \Delta P + p_{\text{shed}},$$

$$T_g\,\dot p_g = -K\,\Delta f - p_g, \qquad T_a\,\dot p_a = -\beta\,\Delta f, \qquad T_b\,\dot p_b = \operatorname{clip}(-K_b\,\Delta f) - p_b,$$

with governors $p_g$ ($T_g = 8$ s), automatic generation control $p_a$ (integral action, $\beta = 680$ MW/Hz, $T_a = 100$ s), the battery $p_b$ (50 MW, $T_b = 0.3$ s), the reserve $R$ capping the upward help, and one block of load shedding $p_{\text{shed}}$ (5% of load) at 59.3 Hz.

This is the single-bus "swing equation" of power-system dynamics. Real studies model each machine and the network between them; lesson A17 (upcoming) uses a small power flow to compare grid-following and grid-forming inverters after a trip.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>How big is inertia on a real grid?</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>During the night of 15 February 2021, ERCOT's measured inertia ranged from 254 to 349 GW·s, and its operators used 100 GW·s as a minimum for operations (FERC–NERC report, 2021, p. 138). ERCOT serves a much larger load than the Plains Grid, so its numbers are larger in proportion.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What the model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>One frequency for the whole region: on a real grid, machines in different places swing against each other along the power lines.</li>
<li>Governors have dead bands and limits, and many plants run with no spare capacity at all.</li>
<li>Real load-shedding programmes cut customers in several smaller steps.</li>
<li>Real AGC also watches the power flowing to neighbouring regions, not only the frequency.</li>
<li>Voltage, which can collapse on its own, is not modelled.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="l3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="restore" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “After a plant trips, governors bring the frequency back to exactly 60 Hz.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Governors stop the fall but leave the frequency a little low; automatic generation control restores 60 Hz over minutes.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="inertia" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “With less inertia online, the frequency falls faster after the same trip.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. The first-second fall rate is proportional to the lost power divided by the stored energy: half the inertia, twice the speed.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="uri" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The February 2021 Texas outages were caused by frozen wind turbines.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Every kind of plant failed: of the 1,045 units with problems, 58% were gas-fired, 27% wind and 6% coal, mostly from freezing and fuel supply (FERC–NERC report, 2021).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="l3">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rocof" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 200 MW plant trips on a grid storing 20 GW·s of rotational energy. How fast does the frequency fall in the first instant?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">0.03 Hz per second</li><li data-value="b">0.3 Hz per second</li><li data-value="c">3 Hz per second</li><li data-value="d">0.6 Hz per second</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>0.3 Hz per second: 60 × 200 ÷ (2 × 20,000) = 0.3. Twice the lost power or half the inertia doubles it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="last" data-answer="d">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which of these acts last after a plant trips?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Inertia</li><li data-value="b">Governors</li><li data-value="c">Automatic generation control</li><li data-value="d">Operators starting another plant to rebuild the reserve</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Operators rebuilding the reserve: this tertiary layer takes ten minutes to hours, so the grid is ready for the next trip.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>In Uri, 1,045 generating units had 4,124 outages, derates or failures to start, about three-quarters of them from freezing or fuel problems. Plants failed faster than operators could restore the reserve, so they cut customers by hand to hold the frequency. Lesson 4 looks at the forecasts that tell operators how much reserve to hold.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>

<li>FERC, NERC and Regional Entity Staff (2021). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2021-11/Cold%20Weather%20Report_%20November%202021.pdf">The February 2021 Cold Weather Outages in Texas and the South Central United States</a> (PDF). Chronology of 15 February, pp. 135–138; load-shedding settings, pp. 44–45; unit outages, p. 15.</li>
<li>EIA (2022). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=54639">U.S. electricity customers averaged seven hours of power interruptions in 2021</a>. Today in Energy.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
